tweets.text:
On tokens and prices per token.

I said I’d write more about this, so here goes: an OpenAI token != another model’s token. We compare AI prices in dollars per million tokens as if a token were a standardized unit, like a gram or a kilowatt-hour. It isn’t. Different models use and produce the exact same text using different numbers of tokens, which means a lower price per token does not necessarily mean a lower bill.

Imagine two identical pizzas. One is cut into 8 slices at $2 each. The other is cut into 16 slices at $1.25 each. The second place advertises cheaper slices, but the whole pizza costs $20 instead of $16. Bummer ... your stomach doesn't actually care about the number of slices you just ate.

I know you are hungry now, but back to tokens. In one small comparison spanning English, technical, multilingual, and numerical text, the tokenizer we use for GPT-5.6 Sol used 766 tokens versus an estimated 1,170 for Claude Opus 5. That's a very significant difference of about 34.5% fewer tokens. You can get the same exact text, but pay for all those extra tokens. The price per token doesn't really tell this story.

Even correcting for tokenizer differences misses the bigger point. What actually matters is price per successful outcome, and for that you can use benchmarks as a starting point, but really you have to try it and measure on your own use cases.

That's all. May the tokens flow.
tweets.summary_zh: OpenAI 的 token（标记）并不是所有模型都一样的，所以单纯比较价格并不准确。就像两份披萨，一份切成8片是$2一片，另一份切16片是$1.25一片，虽然第二份看起来便宜，但整体价格却更高。真正需要关注的是每次成功结果的成本，而不仅仅是每个 token 的价格。

tweets.text:
Last week I’m sitting across a stealth portfolio founder working in a deeply unsexy space (at least from Bay Area standards)..

They’re lamenting about how how some of the critical contracts and partnerships that would give them credibility (and revenue and network effects) are basically stuck at the 1-yard line. This is a massively fragmented market. And this is btw just straight up pure bureaucracy. The champions, terms and everything is lined up. It’s purely a win win situation but summer and one random clause is the issue. And, it might cause them to not reach their ambitious timelines. 

And I’m sitting there smiling and eventually laughing and at some point they ask what’s funny. I tell them “do you know how long it’ll take anyone to do the same thing as you” - and this is with leverage and relationships that they already have. 

And, this in the short term is painful but in the long term becomes such a strong moat. That they’ll look back and laugh why they were worried about a few days when in the long term this is what will make them one of the biggest companies in the world. 

Unnecessary and 996 performative pain is not the moat. But building entrenched software and relationships that take a lot of pain is a moat :)

tweets.text:
I was curious how X is fighting AI slop, so I looked at its open-source algorithm.

It has a behavioral model called TweetSpamBot that analyzes up to 512 recent account actions, looking at signals like posting bursts, quote-post behavior, timing, and normal browsing or dwell between actions.

The model is trained to recognize patterns such as:

→ TWEET_CREATE_BURST
→ QUOTE_TWEET_SPAMMER
→ CONTENT_AMPLIFIER

A high score on the above can feed into an account challenge but doesn't seem to downrank the slop posts themselves.

I think the gap here is that the model doesn’t read the actual post content.

So a sophisticated AI content mill can still post slop all day long:

1. Find viral posts
2. Quote tweet with the same template each time: hook → numbers → backstory → takeaway
3. Repeat 10+ times a day across unrelated topics

If @X doesn't want to become like LinkedIn, I think it should consider looking at accounts that repeatedly turn unrelated viral posts into the same templated quote tweet slop at high volume.

Right now the guardrails above are too easy to bypass.
tweets.summary_zh: 他在说X平台（可能是指Twitter）是如何应对低质量内容的。他分析了一个名叫TweetSpamBot的算法，这个算法看用户的活动，比如发帖频率和时间等，但它并不分析具体的内容。因此，聪明的AI创作工具仍然可以轻松发出低质量的内容。如果X想避免变得像LinkedIn那样，应该关注那些经常把不同的热门帖子变成模板化的低质引用推文的账号。现在的防护措施太容易被绕过了。

tweets.text:
A weird experiment I've been trying the last few weeks is having Claude take over day-to-day maintenance of our apps. Seeing early signs of life that this might be possible.

The setup is straightforward: we have a Slack channel called proj-claude-maintains-apps. In it, Claude Tag runs a bunch of daily routines across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and Agent SDK:

- Crash fuzzer: open the app in a simulator and tap around to find ways to crash it, then root cause and fix the crashes
- Dup unifier: scans the codebase for similar-yet-slightly-divergent abstractions, and puts up PRs to unify them
- Dead-code remover: removes statically unreachable code, and adds logging to suspected dead code to check if it's really dead and if so, remove it the next day
- Abstraction police: fixes leaky abstractions
- a bunch more..

Results have been surprisingly positive. Over the last few weeks, these routines have opened 388 PRs across our repos, 180 of which we merged after Claude Code Review + human review. We're now thinking about how to streamline this to make merging these kinds of mechanical changes easier.

Claude generally gets these PRs right on the first shot, and if it doesn't, we ask Claude to tune its routines so it's better the next day. Sometimes it takes a few days of tuning. 

To try a similar workflow, ask Claude Code or Tag, or create some routines directly at https://t.co/Z70hStEBH6. A few of the actual prompts I used below.

Has anyone experimented with similar workflows?

tweets.text:
Prompt debt is the new tech debt. 

With every model update, you should be cutting at least 50% of your prompts.

Most AI products have bloated prompts that are making your product quality worse.

The typical flow is: model fails at something -> add 10 rules. Tool call fails -> add 10 examples. Output is weird -> add formatting constraints.

3 months later, your system prompt is a novel. 

Meanwhile the model is way smarter and your micro-managey prompts are turning it into a dumb rules machine.
tweets.summary_zh:
“提示债务”（Prompt debt）已经变成了一种新的技术债务（tech debt）。每次更新模型时，最好至少削减一半的提示内容。很多 AI 产品的提示内容太多，反而影响了产品质量。

常见问题是：模型出错了 -> 加十条规则；工具调用失败 -> 加十个例子；输出奇怪 -> 加格式限制。三个月后，你的系统提示内容就像一本小说。

然而，模型本身越来越聪明，而你那些过于复杂的提示反而让它变得像个傻瓜。

tweets.text:
Grok Bot is a fantastic release.. the UX, the design, the onboarding :chefs-kiss:

But I go back and forth on this a lot: Will users (personal and business) want one super agent that holds all the context or sub agents that are designated to do a slice of tasks?

If we treat agents as humans, then the Grok Bot design makes a ton of sense. It allows us to compartmentalize tools, context, outcomes for that person’s division. You reach out to that bot for that specific goal that you have in mind. 

But, if you treat agents as Jarvis, you want a master agent that just gets the job done. It might create and coordinate all the bots (and dare I say the communication/context) that might be needed to do the task. But the interface is 1:1 vs. 1:many. 

My guess is it’ll veer towards the one master agent over time who can then act as an orchestrator who reads / understands the bots you create. But starts narrow as most of the companies are doing it now. 

PS: I understand the core engineering constraints (context windows, tool use, simplicity, cost etc) why companies are choosing task/singular outcomes today. Primarily thinking this from a design / product side.
tweets.summary_zh:
Grok Bot 是个很棒的新产品，它的用户体验和设计都很出色。不过我在想，用户想要一个能同时处理所有事情的“超级助手”，还是更希望有几个专门负责不同任务的小助手呢？

如果把这些助手当作人来看，Grok Bot 的设计就很合理，因为它能针对不同的需求提供具体的工具和信息。但如果把它当成一个类似“人工智能管家”的角色，大家可能更喜欢一个能统筹一切的主助手，它可以协调所有的小助手，完成工作。

我觉得未来可能会倾向于使用一个主助手，它能理解和管理你创建的小助手，但现在大多数公司还是偏向于处理单一任务的设计。

Awesome day in terms of new model releases from both Deepseek and Grok. Both of these new model updates represent huge jumps in capability at insanely low costs. 

This is truly Jevons paradox for AI playing out. By bringing down the cost of AI, demand will continue to accelerate. When I talk to enterprises, they have vastly more use-cases for what they’d like agents to handle than generally what they’re able to budget for today. 

They want agents to scan their codebases for security issues. They want agents to review all their documents. They want agents to process information in a large portion of their workflows. And so on. When we bring down the cost of AI or drive up capability levels, it opens up all new use cases in the enterprises, which drives even greater demand.

This is also great for the applied AI layer. The more choice of models - especially those tuned for different types (or costs) of work - the more value there is in being at the layer that can route and optimize based on the task. Great for the entire stack right now.

tweets.text:
Good post on how to think about FDEs. The key is that FDEs are real and not going away for AI any time soon.

The reason this is happening now at a scale that has never been seen before is because AI is fundamentally about adding a non-deterministic, rapidly changing system to workflows that largely have never been automated before. This looks very little like implementing traditional software.

“If you're building an AI agent for accounting in 2026, there is no established workflow, because literally nobody has ever used one of these. Nobody knows what the user journey looks like — not you, and importantly, not your customer either. They can't tell you what they want, because the thing they'd want doesn't have a shape yet.”

Software has largely always been deterministic and once implemented effectively worked the same for customers. This meant the upfront implementation work was *relatively* uniform across similar customers, and the system wasn’t regularly being upgraded in fundamental ways. 

AI agents are entirely different on nearly every dimension. The customer’s business process has to change to work with agents, there is heavy -necessary- customization to get agents to work in the customers end-state process, evals need to be run constantly, the AI models are constantly changing and updates need to keep getting incorporated, the underlying harness and broader system are often changing due to customer feedback, and much more. 

This is real work for the customer, systems integrators, and the applied AI vendors. Even as AI capabilities improve dramatically, this work remains (or even gets more complicated) given enterprises will just throw increasingly more complex processes at agents. Great time to be an FDE.

tweets.text:
My 5 biggest takeaways from @thenanyu and @delashum from @Linear on how to build a great production agent end to end:

1. The first step is to map the actual workflow.

Identify where work starts, which systems hold context, what actions complete the job, what “done” means, and where a person needs to review. For example, if work starts in Slack, make Slack the on-ramp instead of forcing users to use a separate chatbot.

2. Give agents tools to find context instead of stuffing context into the prompt.

From Jacob: “Give it as little instruction as possible. Give it the tools to load context. Don’t give it context.” Start small, then let the agent pull only the instructions and data it needs for the current task.

3. Start with one frequent job, then expand based on real usage.

Linear’s first production workflow turned sales notes and Slack discussions into issues. The team launched it quietly, watched how people used it, and built the next workflows based on real user behavior instead of a grand spec that covered all possible use cases.

4. Start with the strongest model until the workflow works.

Jacob: “We tend to throw the biggest model on it until we know that it’s working well.” Once you have clear success criteria and evals, test smaller models on narrow jobs. Cost optimization should come after a quality baseline.

5. Turn every real failure into either an eval or a product task.

Linear created two feedback loops from real usage. If the agent had the right tools but behaved badly, the team added that exact case to its evals. If the agent lacked the required tool, it reported the gap so the system could add it to an existing issue for the team to investigate.

If you told someone 3 months ago that a model released by a US company with frontier-class capability would be available as open weights they wouldn’t believe it. 

This is very important because it opens up AI adoption in a range of scenarios that weren’t viable before. Models can be deployed on prem or in the cloud on private infra, which means use-cases in highly regulated domains can be opened up.

You can also now post-train a frontier class model on specific vertical use-cases that need extra levels of performance for their tasks, like in legal, healthcare, and other spaces. You also ensure sovereignty in case any models ever get pulled from the marketplace, which gives users more confidence in deploying in certain mission critical areas.

All of this is great news for the applied AI layer, because this is where you can route work to different model families based on the task at hand. Great time to building at the harness layer given the options available now.

And closed frontier models will still be heavily used both due to simplicity and because you tend to need a mix of capability level for any hard problem, but having open weights in the mix helps defray costs and provides more flexibility. Great news all around.

tweets.text:
One reason why we’re going to get uneven diffusion rates of agents is because different workflows in the enterprise are more or less aligned to continuous, uninterrupted computer work.

A big reason why agentic coding growth has gone completely vertical is because it’s a type of work where economic value is directly correlated with the output of solely digital information, and where the task size can in theory be unbounded in a single session. This means that as AI agents can do larger amounts of work at a time, and as model capability improves on this task type, they can directly be deployed at larger workloads near instantaneously.

Lots of work doesn’t natively have this property in how today’s workflows are designed. A sales rep needs a feedback loop with the customer before they can do additional work for a specific account, a lawyer needs to talk to the client, and a doctor needs to interact with a patient. So large agentic work will likely not look the same as it has in coding, at least by default.

Instead, in many of these domains, the agents will actually need to tie into a workflow that is reengineered for AI.

Matan Grinberg at Factory had a good way of thinking about this on the Training Data podcast: if everyone called in sick tomorrow, token usage would plummet because no one would be there to prompt them. This shows how early we are in agents running in the background for most processes; whereas this should be the majority of volume of agentic work in the future. 

In legal, it will be about processing every contract that comes in, in sales it will be agents that roam through customer records and figure out signals of when to better do outreach, in life sciences research it will be about swarms of agents reading through every test or all research.

To do that these business processes have to be wired up to support agents, as opposed to the vast amounts of manual work that we do today. 

This is the big opportunity right now, but it’s going to diffuse differently from something like agentic coding. Lots of change management, lots of data cleanup, lots of workflow reengineering, and more.

为了解决这个问题，很多企业需要重新设计他们的工作流程，以便与AI更好地配合。这样才能让AI在更多领域发挥作用，虽然这需要大量的变革与调整。现在正是如此改造的好机会！

producthunt.summary_zh: SKI是一款免费语音编程工具，支持Claude Code、Codex等多种编程语言。用户可以通过语音输入代码，简化编程过程，提高效率。该产品旨在让编程变得更便捷。

producthunt.name: Prefactor
producthunt.tagline: Evaluate your AI Agents in real-time
producthunt.summary_zh: Prefactor是一个实时评估AI代理的工具。它能够帮助用户监测和分析AI代理的表现，让用户更好地理解其工作效果。通过这个工具，用户可以即时获取反馈，优化AI代理的使用。

producthunt.name: AdAnt AI
producthunt.tagline: Claude for viral, high-converting social ads
producthunt.summary_zh: AdAnt AI 是一款基于人工智能的工具，专门用于创建具有病毒传播性和高转化率的社交广告。它能够快速生成吸引人的广告文案和创意，帮助用户在社交媒体上提高曝光率和销售转化。简单易用，适合希望优化广告效果的用户。

producthunt.name: Hey Noah
producthunt.tagline: A proactive AI executive assistant for founders
producthunt.summary_zh: Hey Noah是一款主动智能助手，专为创始人设计。它能够管理日程安排、处理邮件和提供业务建议，让用户更高效地专注于公司的发展。通过AI技术，Hey Noah帮助用户简化日常管理任务。

producthunt.name: Wispr Flow Notetaker
producthunt.tagline: Meeting notes that get the details right.
producthunt.summary_zh: Wispr Flow Notetaker是一款会议记录工具，能够自动整理和记录会议内容。它精准捕捉关键信息，帮助用户轻松回顾会议细节。使用简便，提升会议记录效率。

producthunt.name: Lev8
producthunt.tagline: Find, research, and reach the right people
producthunt.summary_zh: Lev8是一款帮助用户寻找和联系合适人选的工具。它允许用户进行深入的研究，以便更好地了解目标群体并与之建立联系。通过Lev8，用户可以简化信息获取和沟通的过程。

producthunt.name: Memmy Agent
producthunt.tagline: Let every AI remember the same you.
producthunt.summary_zh: Memmy Agent 是一款智能工具，可以让不同的人工智能系统记住你的个性化信息。通过它，你的偏好和特点将被同步到多个AI中，从而提供更加个性化的服务。使用 Memmy Agent，你无需重复输入信息，AI将更好地了解你。

producthunt.name: Adomate
producthunt.tagline: Turn data into winning ads. At scale.
producthunt.summary_zh: Adomate是一款广告自动化工具，能够将数据转化为高效的广告。它帮助用户在大规模上创造和优化广告，提高投放效果。通过智能分析和实时调整，Adomate让广告投放更加精准和省时。

producthunt.name: Dograh
producthunt.summary_zh: Dograh 是一个开源的 VAPI 替代方案，旨在提供灵活的 API 解决方案。用户可以使用它创建、管理和测试 API，简化开发过程，提高效率。这个工具支持多种编程语言，方便开发者集成。

producthunt.name: Coldtea.ai
producthunt.summary_zh: Coldtea.ai 是一款智能软件工具，它可以自动化软件的运行和管理流程。用户只需简单设置，系统就能自主完成复杂任务，提高工作效率。

producthunt.name: AI Search Console
producthunt.tagline: Prompt analytics and citation mapping for AI search
producthunt.summary_zh: AI Search Console 是一款用于分析AI搜索的工具，能帮助用户了解搜索提示的效果和引用的来源。它提供数据分析和可视化图谱，便于优化搜索结果和提高搜索效率。
